content: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions. {{v:2}} Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin. {{v:3}} For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me. {{v:4}} Against you, and you only, I have sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight, so you may be proved right when you speak, and justified when you judge. {{v:5}} Behold, I was born in iniquity. My mother conceived me in sin. {{v:6}} Behold, you desire truth in the inward parts. You teach me wisdom in the inmost place. {{v:7}} Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean. Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow. {{v:8}} Let me hear joy and gladness, that the bones which you have broken may rejoice. {{v:9}} Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all of my iniquities. {{v:10}} Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me. {{v:11}} Don’t throw me from your presence, and don’t take your Holy Spirit from me. {{v:12}} Restore to me the joy of your salvation. Uphold me with a willing spirit. {{v:13}} Then I will teach transgressors your ways. Sinners will be converted to you. {{v:14}} Deliver me from the guilt of bloodshed, O God, the God of my salvation. My tongue will sing aloud of your righteousness. {{v:15}} Lord, open my lips. My mouth will declare your praise. {{v:16}} For you don’t delight in sacrifice, or else I would give it. You have no pleasure in burnt offering. {{v:17}} The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart. {{v:18}} Do well in your good pleasure to Zion. Build the walls of Jerusalem. {{v:19}} Then you will delight in the sacrifices of righteousness, in burnt offerings and in whole burnt offerings. Then they will offer bulls on your altar.

facets.text: The psalm opens by grounding the plea for forgiveness entirely in God's own character rather than in any merit of the penitent. Mercy is sought "according to your loving kindness" and "the multitude of your tender mercies"—the sinner's only appeal is the abundance of divine compassion. This teaches that forgiveness is pure gift flowing from God's steadfast covenant love (hesed), not something wrung from Him by human worthiness.
facets.question: On what basis can a sinner dare to ask God for forgiveness?

facets.text: The psalmist confesses "Against you, and you only, I have sinned," recognizing that every sin, however it wounds others, is ultimately an offense against God whose will is the measure of good and evil. He willingly justifies God's verdict—"so you may be proved right when you speak"—accepting divine judgment as righteous rather than protesting it. True contrition acknowledges guilt honestly and vindicates God's justice instead of excusing the self.
facets.question: Why is all sin ultimately committed against God?

facets.text: The confession "I was born in iniquity; my mother conceived me in sin" reaches beneath particular acts to a wounded condition inherited from the very beginning of life. The Catholic tradition reads this as a scriptural witness to original sin—the fallen state into which every human being is born—which is why the psalmist knows his need for cleansing runs deeper than any single transgression. It is not a condemnation of marriage or conception but a recognition of humanity's universal need for redemption.
facets.question: Does the Bible teach that we are born already affected by sin?

facets.text: The prayer "Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean; wash me, and I will be whiter than snow" draws on the ritual of sprinkling used to cleanse from defilement in the Law. Catholic tradition sees here a foreshadowing of baptismal washing and the purifying blood of Christ, of which the hyssop and water were figures. What Levitical rites could only signify outwardly, the grace of the New Covenant accomplishes inwardly, making the soul whiter than snow.
facets.question: What does the sprinkling with hyssop point to in the sacraments of the New Covenant?

facets.text: "Create in me a clean heart, O God; renew a right spirit within me" asks not merely for pardon but for interior re-creation, using the verb of God's original creative act. Forgiveness of guilt is completed by a positive renewal of the person, a new beginning that only God can author. This anticipates the promise of a new heart and a new spirit fulfilled in the grace of regeneration and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit.
facets.question: What does it mean to ask God to create a clean heart within us?

facets.text: The plea "Don't take your Holy Spirit from me" and "Restore to me the joy of your salvation" reveals that sin's deepest wound is the loss of communion with God and the joy that flows from it. The penitent longs not only to escape punishment but to be restored to God's presence and animated by a willing spirit. Repentance aims at reconciled friendship with God, and its fruit is a joy that overflows into teaching sinners and drawing them to conversion.
facets.question: What is the deepest thing lost through sin and restored through repentance?

facets.text: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" declares that the interior disposition of humble sorrow is the offering God truly desires above ritual sacrifice. External worship without a contrite heart is empty; God looks first to the heart. This does not abolish sacrifice but reveals its soul, teaching that authentic worship must be inwardly true.
facets.question: What sacrifice does God most desire from a repentant person?

facets.text: The psalm closes by praying that God build the walls of Jerusalem and again delight in offerings on the altar, showing that the sinner's restoration is bound up with the flourishing of the whole covenant people and its worship. Personal repentance is not merely private; it opens into the renewal of Zion and the restoration of right sacrifice. Catholic tradition sees this fulfilled in the heavenly Jerusalem and the pure offering of Christ, in which the contrite heart and true sacrifice are finally united.
facets.question: How is personal repentance connected to the restoration of God's people and their worship?

facets.text: The petition "Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise" acknowledges that even the ability to praise God rightly is itself a grace that must be given. The forgiven sinner becomes a witness whose renewed tongue sings of God's righteousness and teaches others His ways. Redemption thus overflows into proclamation, so that the mercy received becomes mercy announced.
facets.question: Why does the forgiven sinner need God to open his lips for praise?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Psalm 51, the great penitential Miserere, pleads for forgiveness grounded in God's mercy, confesses sin and the fallen human condition, and asks for interior re-creation, the restored Holy Spirit, and true worship in a contrite heart bound to the renewal of Zion.

[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Forgiveness is sought purely on the basis of God's steadfast covenant love and abundant mercy, not human merit.
[MORAL | explicit]: All sin is ultimately an offense against God; true contrition confesses guilt honestly and vindicates God's justice.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: Being "conceived in sin" witnesses to original sin, the universal fallen condition requiring redemption, not a condemnation of conception.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: Cleansing with hyssop and washing whiter than snow foreshadow baptismal washing and the purifying blood of Christ.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: "Create in me a clean heart" asks for interior re-creation and renewal by the Holy Spirit, not merely pardon of guilt.
[DEVOTIONAL | explicit]: Sin's deepest wound is loss of communion and joy with God; repentance aims at restored friendship and overflows in converting others.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: A broken and contrite heart is the sacrifice God desires; authentic worship must be inwardly true.
[TYPOLOGICAL | inferential]: Personal restoration is joined to the flourishing of Zion and right sacrifice, fulfilled in Christ's pure offering and the heavenly Jerusalem.
[DEVOTIONAL | traditional]: Even praise is grace; God must open the sinner's lips so received mercy becomes proclaimed mercy.
